Quote: blue_tetris, April 21, 2007 02:45 am
Quote: Atilla, 2007-04-21T02:04:26Z
And do you need high-powered automatic weapons, particularly handguns, for hunting or sport shooting?

No. And I never said all usage was sport or agriculture, although many people do hunt with pistols and hunting pistols are of higher caliber than typical handguns.

Quote: Atilla, 2007-04-21T02:04:26Z
Restricting such weapons will have no impact on those who shoot for sport, nor will it have any impact on farmers who "feel safe" because they own a shotgun. If this constitutes a large proportion of gun owners, so much the better!

Yeah, but it's not entirely about that demographic. It's at least, in part, for the people who should be able to exercise the liberty to defend themselves with a handgun. No matter how great the percentage of agricultural- or sport-oriented handgun usage is, there exists a minority of non-criminals who wish to defend themselves with handguns and that minority should be acknowledged.

Quote: Atilla, 2007-04-21T02:04:26Z
Furthermore, agricultural and hunting firearms generally have a small clip (if any at all) and low firing rate, at least in Australia. If people "feel safe" because they own such weapons, doesn't that imply that automatic and semi-auto weapons aren't necessary for most people to feel they have adequate ability to defend themselves?

They probably aren't necessary for most people to feel safe. In the same vein, alcohol probably isn't necessary for most people to enjoy themselves. Gas-guzzling cars and skydiving are unnecessary (and certainly risky) vices to make a person feel more self-important. There exist many many things that go beyond the realms of necessity to suffice some basic human need. In the end, it's a matter of liberty. It's not about finding the cheapest or safest possible factor of human satisfaction. It's about choice.

No one needs to bungee jump to feel like a man, no one needs to drink to forget, no one needs to speak out about his radical opinions to feel appreciated, and no one needs to keep a semi-automatic next to the bed to ease her paranoia about the frightening world beyond the window. But should people have the liberty to do these things? I think so.

I'm sure their are other arenas of human experience which you feel should not be inhibited in an effort to stuff more padding into the walls of our social asylum and tighten the straightjacket to keep us from flailing about. Why isn't the liberty to be secure worth pursuing to the extent of other such positive liberties?

At what point, though, do those things become a breach upon other people's liberties? When 25% of semi-automatic gun owners kill people? 50%? 75%? 100%? At what point does preservation of human life and everyone else's right to exist trump a person's "right" to drink and carry a gun? Now, of course, drinking and carrying guns aren't at fault, and I see where you say that people should have the liberty to do both. But unless we can police the bad parts - In this case, drunk driving and gun murders - Then what else is there to do? Should people have the liberty to bungee? Certainly. Should they have the liberty to drink? Should they have the liberty to own guns? Absolutely. It's protected in the constitution. But should people have the liberty to use said guns in murders, drink and drive, and so on? I think we can all agree that the answer there is "no."

So, point being, we can't police anti-murder laws or anti-drunk driving laws to any further success. So what do we do, continue to accept and support the evils that come along with these liberties? What other choice would there be beyond beginning to prohibit said liberties in order to preserve something larger and more important to us all? What's more important to us, the liberty to carry a gun, or the preservation of a person's liberty to live without intervention from an outside and negative force? Should we eliminate a person's right to defending themselves with a firearm if they so choose? Does anyone need to defend themselves with a firearm if lesser means would be as effective in nearly all situations? Should we eliminate their liberty to their own defense?

Quote: Tsukatu, 2007-04-25T05:18:53Z
Free will can't exist in conjunction with an omniscient being. There's a thread about this. But even if free will somehow existed as well, I just can't see how you think that anything you're saying addresses what I've been saying. Let me put this another way:
In the history of mankind, there has been at least one person who has died an atheist, and who was an atheist when he died because every influence around him convinced him that God couldn't possibly exist and that God was in fact a malevolent psychopath. At least one such person has existed since the dawn of time. That person is now in Hell because He rejected Jesus Christ. The problem here, if you haven't spotted it, is that God knew that this man's life would be like this. He knew that the man would make his own choices, but that the influences around him would turn him into an atheist. The man's faith never stood a chance, and it wasn't his fault. And now he's in Hell. Given that these are the circumstances, that the man will go to Hell (and it's not at all his fault), the only thing that can turn him back to the truth is God's direct intervention. But God didn't intervene. He let the man suffer in Hell, even though he was blameless.
If one such person has ever existed, your God is not omnibenevolent, and He does not love all of His children, because that innocent man that He let go to Hell was a child He clearly did not love.

The thought of free will versus omni-potency is, in fact, a misrepresentation. There doesn't necessarily need to be an either or situation with it. The situation itself assumes that God has interests and is somehow dependant upon the things that occur in this reality, and vice-versa. Considering that we can't grasp the concept of what a deity's intentions might be, I don't think that we can say whether he is or is not omnibenevolent, or whether that God has love or caring, understanding, interests, motives, reasons, or anything else invested in this reality of ours. And the same goes for Obby, as well. We can't debate what God's motives might be unless we were to know them.

Other people don't know what to believe, and they half-assedly work on the riddle. They've been told the answer before, but they might not recall it correctly. #315822 7 2007-04-25T20:55:32Z Kablizzy
Assuming that nothing ridiculously overpowered could be used in either situation (For instance, Star Trek shields being able to block all Star Wars Weapons, or anything like the Genesis Machine being able to be fired), then yeah, Star Wars would absolutely break some Star Trek Ass.

Then again, something like the Federation isn't mobilised for all-out war, whereas the Empire is, and always has been. They're war-like, they're like Genghis Khan - They maraud in, destroy everything, and maraud out, there's not much that more civilized and less militant civilisations can do about it. Think of the single Borg cube that made it to Earth during the TNG years. That one Borg Cube went to school on the entire federation.

Now, if we're talking the Borg Collective against the Galactic Empire, then it's an entirely different story.

Furthermore, Star Wars is more of a steam-punk feel, where the battles and technology is a lot more dirty and real, whereas Star Trek has a more mystical feel to it. Star Trek is focused a lot more on the personal scale, whereas Star Wars is crafted for the large-scale Empirical feel. Think of how many ships the Empire would have access to as opposed to the Federation and allies.

It's just that - All things aside, and assuming blasters do some damage to Star Trek shields, a single Star Cruiser could focus more firepower on one spot in space than most of the Federation could muster. I mean, yeah, Tie Fighters might not do much alone, but again, assuming they damage shields, a Star Trek Ship wouldn't last too long against a whole fleet of TIE fighters - Take a look at how much damage The Enterprise's shields suffered against such things as a Ferengi freighter - Lightly-armed ships can knock the Enterprise's shields down to 30-some percent with only a hit or two. Give it a couple thousand shots from Tie-Fighters spread across the entire fleet (Not to mention Death Stars and all the other ships that would be entering combat), and there's just really not much the federation could end up doing. If the Federation ships were maneuverable enough to dodge all shots to come from the Empire, I don't think it's a fair comparison to make in the first place.

Hand-to-hand combat wouldn't be much better for the Federation, either. Just looking at combat, most Federation officers are only armed with simple phasers, and could only muster a certain amount of firepower per ship. Given the notion of forcefields, though, you're right, so Darth Maul can hop onto your ship, I doubt he has the skill to Force away seventy-two force fields over twelve decks and then fight an entire ship's worth of phasers. Then again, Death Star just blew your planet up. Oh, darn, there goes your home, have fun floating in space until you die.

Now, if we are assuming that federation and allied ships have that maneuverability so as not to get hit (Things like being able to fire photon torpedos while coming out of warp, fire a couple phaser blasts, and then back into warp), then The Star Trek ships are relatively untouchable.

So, putting the Borg into the equation tips the scales in favour of the Star Trek universe. The federation and Klingon and allied empires would still take heavy damage, I think, but given the entirety of the Borg entering the fray, I don't think there's any way that any number of firepower could get around the Borg's shield modulation. All it would take is a single blaster shot, and then the shields modulate throughout the entire Borg empire, and that's Good Game.

Not sure what else I wanted to say, but given the situations outlined above, that's about the up and down of it.

#317269 8 2007-05-01T02:40:56Z Kablizzy
Mmkay. I'm going to critique these like I would a Legacy level, hopefully this helps -

The Golden Age: Way, way too much gold. And no enemies makes this a tad tedious. With that said, jumping around is fun as Hell. Neat tileset to toy with, but yeah, adding some challenges and lessening the gold a lot would help immensely. Also, be careful to click out of the loading textbox in NED. You NaN'd a bounceblock (Which means the code bugs and it appears outside of the playable area).

Namesake: Nice lettering, but again, more enemies, less ambient objects. Try and go for a strategic placement of things - As things are with this, things look randomly placed.

Far-Flung: Again, very nice concept with the playable N-Art. This one is the best of the playable N-Arts.

Tributary: Nice play on words for the title. As with the first three, I'd say they're more meant for looking at than for playing - these first four, at least, would go better on NUMA than here on the forums. As for the gold halo, neat effect, but for a playable map, s'just way, way too much.

Supersize: I think these would all be better as non-playable N-arts, for play purposes. There are just way too many objects in these maps for them to be considered playable. I think they'd be better suited as plain eye-candy.

Optical Delusion: Ah, here we go. For a strictly playable map, way too many objects, mostly the gold. The gameplay gets tedious because it's such a large map, so I think this would do well as a smaller map (Perhaps even half as big). Great theme to it, and pretty good for an action level.

Dodge 'em: Nice little action map here, but again, way way too much gold. Enemy placement was good.

Cross Country: Neat idea, but it seems like you wanted to make three distinct maps out of this.

Madness Interactive: Very cool map - You have some things to learn about placement and aesthetics, but you're well on your way to making some good maps. Again, watch the textbox when you're loading your maps, you NaN'd two objects - Gold and a Mine, so be sure to click outside of the textbox before you load. Beyond the room full o' gold, this was quite fun. Just keep at it - And if you need further clarification, don't be afraid to ask, I'll be glad to help.

1. Do you think citizens should have the rights to criticize elected officials like the president, governor, or city officials?

2. Do you think burning the American flag in anger or protest is an acceptable form of free speech or do you see it as an unacceptable act?

Not really, no. I've never understood what burning the flag could ever possibly represent in the way of a positive point. As I see it, it's always done in outrage and in hatred, and that's not really acceptable.

Quote: DemonzLunchBreak, 2007-05-09T01:55:58Z
3. Do you think religious beliefs that people hold sacred should be open to comedy, criticism, or insults?

Comedy, sure. Everyone should be able to laugh at themselves and at others. I'll make a Muhammad joke from time to time, Criticism and insults, no, not really.

Quote: DemonzLunchBreak, 2007-05-09T01:55:58Z
4. Do you think books that contain harsh language or controversial subject matter (sexual refrences, fantasy/witch craft, violence, etc...) should be banned from school libraries?

Not unilaterally. It should vary by age of the students that have access.

Quote: DemonzLunchBreak, 2007-05-09T01:55:58Z
5. Do you think that speakers or groups, whose views may be unpopular or hateful should be allowed to speak their mind?

Yes. That is the core of free speech, not this other tripe. People should have the freedom to be heard, and have their ideas considered.

Quote: DemonzLunchBreak, 2007-05-09T01:55:58Z
6. Would you support limiting the jokes people can tell if it would help to decrease insensitive comments about racism, sexism, and intolerance (No ethnic jokes, blonde jokes, jokes about lifestyles, disabilities, etc...) ?

Quote: DemonzLunchBreak, 2007-05-09T01:55:58Z
7. Do you think that singers/bands should be prevented from writing or performing songs that have profanity or other controversial lyrics in them?

Shit no. Profanity is different from racist / hateful speech.

Quote: DemonzLunchBreak, 2007-05-09T01:55:58Z
8. Should the internet be regulated so that dangerous, obscene, hateful, pornographic, etc... websites would not be permitted?

YES. YES YES YES YES YES. GOD YES. Not so much that they shouldn't be *permitted*, per se, but definitely, and most certainly regulated. In fact, I want to work on an initiative to submit to Congress some day that regulates the entire Internet. The Internet was never created with security or rules or standards in mind, and it needs to have them, desperately. Boundaries and guidelines over what, where, who, why, and how need to be implemented, and the sooner the better.

#319975 21 2007-05-10T03:25:53Z Kablizzy
Is dendrophilia a choice? Is being a furry a choice? Mmm? Would it be a choice to be a furry if the notion never existed? Is it possible to be attracted to inanimate objects? Is it possible to be a Heliophile? Can you be attracted to a planet? Is it possible to be attracted to concepts?

If the answer to the above is "yes," then it logically follows that attraction isn't a byproduct of the desire to procreate, and sexual desire and attraction must not be tied in to reproduction. In this instance, yes, it is possible that being homosexual is a genetic trait.

If the answer to those above questions is "no," then it can lead also to the idea that sexual desire and attraction *might* not be tied in to reproduction. But in this instance, it might also follow (And is more likely in this instance) that attraction is indeed tied directly to reproduction and procreation. In this instance, there would have to be an alternate explanation as to why homosexuality manifests, whether genetic, psychological, environmental, or otherwise in origin. I feel as though this is the more likely of the two situations.

In either case, this is the one area of debate that my proverbial jury is still out on. On the one hand, I don't want to be insensitive, but on the other, I see no genetic benefit to being gay, and thus, there's no way for me to claim that it isn't a choice. Thus, I'm not entirely sold on the thought that it is an entirely genetic thing. If it is, there's a good possibility that it is strictly a deficient gene combination that either manifests via environment, psychologically, or as I said above, a gene combination.

So, no, not a choice, as a blanket statement - Some people do choose it (Women who hate men so much that they "give women a shot," for instance), but as a whole, no, not a choice.

#321372 13 2007-05-15T10:34:36Z Kablizzy
0 is neutral. The number represents the concept of "having no value".

1 is a number representing something that has value; in this case 1, but any number represents value. This makes it distinct from 0, which has no value.

A "number" that is infinitely small added up to 0 means that 0 now has value. In this sense, 0 CANNOT equal "infinitely small".

As 0 is not equal to "infinitely small", .999~ cannot be equal to 1. 3/3 is equal to 1, of course. But when you start doing 1/3 = .333~ you're making a flawed representation of the CONCEPT 1/3. This equation is the only really "clean" way to express it.

So when you do .333~ + .333~ you're working with the flaw (in that the number does not correctly represent the concept) and that exposes itself in .999~ = 1.

As LV said, it's an axiom. .333~ does not equal 1/3, in the technical sense. It is the closest to 1/3 that you can get, represented numerically, but it does not equal 1/3. It equals the closest standard numerical representation thereof. But let's say you take 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3, in fractional terms. When you go to make 1 from that, it's always represented, numerically, like this;

.33 + .33 + .34

Where's that entire extra .01 come from? That's the key to this. .999~ will never equal 1 in the technical sense.

Mmkay. Time to end this.

Let's begin. Take 0.9 for a minute. Add a 9 to that. Does that equal 1? Add another 9. Add another. One more? Do another. Do any of those equal 1? No. And they never will. No amount of adding another 9 to that string will ever add up to another whole. Taking your example in kind, you're right, that last 1 at the string of zeros will never pop up. By the same token, one of those 9s won't ever roll over to a 10 at any point.

Here's where the problem comes in: You substitute, in your equation, .999... for x. You then set x equal to the equational representation of 3/3. As I said above, it's a split in concepts - 1/3 is equal to 1/3, and .333... is equal to .333. When you use the concept of 1/3 (Which has no true numerical representation), you misrepresent the *concept* of 1/3 as a numeral. While it may seem intutitive that .333... equals 1/3 (After all, that's what we're taught in elementary school), it's only the closest thing. There is no 4 at the end of that string of 3s, and thus, no matter how close it comes, it never rolls over. It just always gets closer. And that's the concept of infinity. The second that number rolls over, it ceases being infinitely close, because it is no longer infinitely close, it is. Thus, Infinitely close != Infinitely close.

Look at it this way, and let's try it on a calculator...

1 - .6 = .4
1 - .66 = .34
1 - .6666 = .3334
1 - .6666666666 = .3333333334

If you drag it out you get infinite sixes, infinite threes. How can you have a four _after_ an infinite number of threes? By definition, _infinite_ never ends. You can't put something after the end of something that never ends.

The problem is that the decimal representation system is not equipped to represent things like this. Whenever the words "infinite", "infinitesimal", or "irrational" come into play, the decimal system is inherently inadequate. That's all there is to it. And to understand this, you have to realize that logically, this is wrong.

This is not a limitation of math, or numbers, or anything of the sort. It's a limitation solely of the decimal system we use to represent these quantities visually. Representation is separate from concept. So, what the number is represented by is entirely separate from the concept of the number. I'm speaking concepts here, I'm no mathematician.

There are a great many directions this discussion can take. But at the heart of it is the fact that mathematics is built not on fundamental truths, but on postulates and working assumptions. Such things are necessary in order to have progress. Changing the postulates and assumptions yields work that is just as valid and valuable. But one must recognize that the foundations are different, and so results can't be transferred directly.

So, the issue here is context. I'm speaking of the literal form of this number (Concept), and you're speaking about the technical form of this number (Representation). In order for math to work, on any level, you must *represent* the number as a spot on the number line. Since the *concept* of 0.999~ can never be represented on that line, it must fall somewhere, and that somewhere that it falls is at 1. Is that any fault of the concept? Certainly not. It's all a problem with notation, and how the number has to be represented. Solely because we, as a race, use this little thing called mathematics to solve our numerical equations doesn't mean that there isn't something out there that transcends it. There is this concept out there that says, "What number is closest between 0.9 and 1? Why, that's 0.99, of course. And between that and 1? 0.999! Correct!" Do that an infinite number of times. Do you ever reach a conclusion? No, and why? Simply because you can't reach the conclusion. That's the idea of infinity, it never ceases. It never rolls upward that one itty little bit. And that's where the math comes in. Math says, in the most literal, plain terms possible, "This equals 1." Does it, in actuality? No, but to keep it clean, Math says "Yes, because it's just thaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaat close."

The quantity "infinity", represented here as the tilde, is not compatible with arithmetic operators, unless we apply limits, which by definition changes the rules a little. And that's where our debate comes in. Really, Infinity can't be plugged in or calculated. Mathematically, it can, and the only way that math can do that is through limits.

DLB: You have to think of it in terms of a limit in order to calculate it, yes. And that's the entire point. Within our concept of mathematics, in order for mathematics to exist and work, certain things need to bend a tad, like the concept of infinity. Really, infinity never stops. I don't think it's all that easy to wrap one's head around. It never, ever stops doing what it does.

Edit: And to be clear, Critical Thinking really has no place in mathematics. I'm no mathematician, and I don't pretend to be. What this argument is - Is a step outside of how we think in an attempt to expand our minds. The concept of infinity simply means that when you think you're done counting, and you can say "Woo! I've reached 1! This is the point where I've reached 1!" the answer is, "Nope, keep going, you're not there yet." Forever and ever and ever.

#15274 1 2007-05-18T08:09:07Z Kablizzy
Dronies Nominations 2007 are CLOSED!

Dronies nominations for December 1, 2006 - November 30, 2007 are now open! All we need is your NUMA name (If you don't have a NUMA name for some reason, your username here is fine), and your list of Nominations - It would be preferable if you nominated something for each category. You most certainly don't have to - but the more nominations we get for each of these, the better the results will be at the end of the year. Results will be tallied through raw data, and will be reviewed by the Legacy Team for fraudulent entries. Now, we have a couple changes this season, so I'd like to take a moment to explain those -

N Highscorer of the Year - This has replaced N Player of the Year, since people got confused last year and were simply nominating their favourite person. For this, you should nominate the name of the person.

Comic of the Year - We're deciding to revive this one, but there will be one stipulation - You may not vote for The Real N. The Real N is pretty much a Legacy-run comic now, and from the number of pseudo-votes we've had for it in my casual discussion, I think it would be unfair to the other comic makers to include it. Any other comic is up for nomination.

N Community Recognition Award - This is a new award category for this year, and for all years to come. This is the community's equivalent of the Mare and Raigan Award for Contribution to the Community. It allows you guys to pay respects to the deserved of the community. Nominate here just like you would any other category - For a person in the community.

With those out of the way, Nominations are open, and please, discuss as much as you wish about them in this thread. I would like for everyone to encourage nominations throughout the second half of this year, and not do things last-minute.

Categories

Action Map of the Year
DDA of the Year
Fan Programme of the Year
Map Maker of the Year
Map Series of the Year
Most Innovative Use of Objects or Tiles
N Art of the Year
N Highscorer of the Year
Comic of the Year
Puzzle Map of the Year
Race Map of the Year
Run of the Year
Survival Map of the Year
Tileset of the Year
N Community Recognition Award

And with that in mind, Vote Away!

You can add or change nominations, yes - the last map/author submitted from you is the copy that I will keep. So, when you submit, let's say you submit your favorite author and your favorite action map, but later change your mind on your favorite author vote, your favorite action map vote will stand, and your favorite author vote will be the second one submitted.

With that said, try to keep ideas in a .txt file, and make an attempt to submit all at once - The less submissions I have to organize and sort through, the easier finals will be this December (Having to take 6 finals and sort through Dronies nominations is not going to be pleasant as-is, so every little bit that I can get to help out is good).

Beyond that, you all have notepads in your accounts here (Under my profile) that you can save links into, and come November, I can remind you all that you may have put stuff there, and you can always just post here some prospects that you think are worthy, and want to sort through later - Just make sure to edit old posts first.

#327277 27 2007-06-04T06:47:04Z Kablizzy
Edit: Man, this really comes across as me being an asshole. I don't mean it, I'm trying to give more constructive criticism than anything. Sorry if it comes across as otherwise.

Alrighty, I just played through the pack, and I have some praise and some criticism.

First off, the mapping was about average. The map length, overall, was a tad too long, and the difficulty was on the high side of average, but the problem with the difficulty was more that it didn't change throughout the pack. It just kinda stayed the same. And the gold patterns staying similar through the pack kinda turned me off a bit.

Secondly, you guys had some AMAZING ideas here. Some of the tilesets absolutely freakin' blew me away, and some of the map names were unbelievably creative. I loved the idea behind this, and if it were executed better, this might be among my favourite packs.

But here's the bad part, guys. The organization was atrocious. It was really, really terrible. The pack itself comes in a migraine-inducing clump that screws up the entire pack. When you load the pack into userlevels, it bugs half of the maps, and the pack name doesn't even appear on all of the maps. Some of the maps have NaN errors, some include the ninja being automatically killed, and some have the ninja outside of the map area. The mapper's names are scattered about, some of the maps are labeled as action, some Action, some as the author name, and some maps don't appear at all. Now, when I say organization, I don't just mean the formatting. I mean playtesting. I think that in order to put a quality pack out, you've got to do some form of going through the maps and saying, "hey, I didn't quite like this part, maybe you should do this with the map," and getting everyone's feedback from there. I mean, the reason it takes Legacy 9 months to pump a pack out isn't because we're mapping the whole time - We're tweaking the whole time. All of this bad stuff that I mentioned would've been caught with a little extra time spent on the after-thought.

But more importantly, on the organization front, most of the maps are... not so much boring... as they are just kinda unimpressive. Quite a few of them come across as forgettable. As I said above, the ideas are absolutely amazing, the themes are fantastic, but there seems to be something to each map that didn't feel finished. They all felt like they started out with the right idea in mind, and then veered off when the sixteen chaser drones and 48 mines were put in. It's one of those things where I can see the tileset, and I know where the mapper wanted to take the map, but then I look at the objects, and turn my head to the side and go, "Why did he do that with the map?" Y'know?

You guys had the right idea, for sure, but it didn't quite seem to make it to the finish line.

Now, for the good news. I think you guys could improve this back a whole bunch, and perhaps re-release it sometime down the road. Like I said, this could be a great pack with some (a lot) of tweaking.

#327285 30 2007-06-04T08:35:40Z Kablizzy
Yeah, in hindsight, I don't mean to come down on you guys, I just think that this pack had so much more potential than what ended up coming out of it.

And, this gave me an idea. Perhaps you guys could turn this thread into a giant community project - Something that everyone can get in on and provide input with. That'd be a fun time (For me, at least, dunno about everyone else).

frets: That's exactly where you went wrong, I think. You didn't want to be in on the project, and as much as I hate to say it, it showed. I think you only had a few maps in the pack, and the ones that you submitted were grainy and felt unfinished. They were, as a whole, too long, and too complex for the eyes. Look at the Metanet maps. I'm going to do an article soon called "Analysing the MetaMap", because there are a handful of things predominant in most of them;

Patterns - Metanet Utilizes a lot of patterns. Pattern recognition is absolutely huge in aesthetics, and is a big part of what is and is not appealing to the eye. Now, having one or two things that shoot off from this isn't a bad thing, but the only maps from this pack that I remember are the ones that included patterns.

Simplicity - Minimalism makes packs. Long maps don't belong in map packs. Packs, more often than not, are meant to be played as a whole, rather than just a conglomeration of maps. If it were just a smattering of different maps, you'd be better suited to submit them to NUMA as a series.

Physics - One of the lesser-thought themes in a Metanet map is the idea of Physics that they use. They use a ton of jumps, but not in the same way as NUMA authors do. Metanet uses downward jumps, making landings difficult to stick. They do this in a few other ways, too, but one of the most predominant things that their maps accomplish is, basically, to showcase their physics engine!

Space - I still haven't mastered space management, but Metanet does it beautifully. Their tilesets draw the eye to the action, and away from the empty space - In fact, in most of their maps, you don't notice empty space. This is perhaps the trickiest thing to get the hang of once you become an established mapper, but it's perhaps the most rewarding to get a good hold of, and most NUMA mappers (I'd say a vast majority, even) don't even have the concept at all.

I... In fact, let me link you guys to a little something we began on a while ago. It's not finished, but it should give a couple ideas for ya'll;

Map Theory (It all seems like really basic stuff, but you'd be surprised at how few people actually understand how this stuff affects gameplay).

Edit Edit: man, I just realized how awesome Map Theory was going to be. I've gotta pick that up again.

#327388 38 2007-06-04T18:29:20Z Kablizzy
I do want to retract that point l_d. It's not that long maps don't have a place in map packs - They do. They really do. What I was getting at was that long maps need to be mixed well with shorter, simpler maps, but the type of NUMA longmap that we've come to grow used to is strictly outside of a pack setting. Which is entirely what this pack here was. And more complex maps absolutely ruin flavour and kill theme - The maps need to be unique and memorable, and when you come across the sixteenth map with eight switches, all hidden under bounceblocks, all guarded by 8 chainguns and seeker drones, smattered with mines, and on and on and on and on and on, it gets so repetitious. You have to strike a good balance between short and long maps, simplistic and complex ones, and so on.

In either case, take Instructables (Which everyone needs to read) that Mare and Raigan put up this morning. I'll quote a couple parts thereof here in a bit. But the point is that simple maps don't need to be short, and don't need to blow by. And good simple maps don't. Simplicity in a map doesn't dictate anything about the map's gameplay - It just takes skill as an author to utilize the simplicity in the right ways. Minimalism and unique execution are keys in what makes a good episodic map. If you make long maps, you're not necessarily a bad author, you're just a NUMA author. You don't do packs as well, because you can't grasp the idea of minimalism and simplicity. Look at every Mare and Raigan level - They do minimalism better than anyone. So, confusing difficulty and distance with aesthetic principles is where I think we're going wrong here. Simple maps have a perfect place in packs, particularly episodic packs, because the pack is meant to be played as a whole, rather than as 124 really long, grueling maps. That's why Alexi's portion stood head and shoulders above the rest in this pack, the stuff he did was unique, and simplistic. It embraced minimalism, and it took simplicity to an exciting level. However, somewhere in the middle, too many objects and too much of the same idea got involved, and that ruined most of the maps. That's what I mean by minimalism - Each of Alexi's maps tried to do too much, and that ruined it. So anyway, on to the quotes.

Quote
Remember to focus on minimalism: too many entities or too many types of entity gets distracting fast. Limit yourself, as this will give your level the most punch. You can't go wrong with more punch.

Quote
A good N level should be easy on the eyes -- embrace minimalism. Good N levels incorporate balance in terms of positive and negative space (as created by the tiles and lack thereof), position and number of objects and tiles, and symmetry.

Quote
Because the design of the tiles is so strong, the objects have been placed in an orderly and minimal fashion, so as to keep the focus on the tiles, and not distract the eye.

Quote
Repetition of pattern and shape throughout a level will give it a clean and consistent look.

Quote
Although there are several subtle changes to the pattern, the repetition of strongly contrasting shapes in this map disguises differences, giving the level a clean and overall consistent look.

Quote
Note the symmetry in spacing of these columns, the consistency in doorway placement, and the general balance of the design.

Quote
Juxtaposition of several styles can quickly clutter up a design.

Quote
Note how the thwumps were positioned according to a pattern.

Quote
This map contains more object and enemy types than we've seen so far, and yet it manages to remain visually uncluttered due to its use of vast untiled space and simple, concise tiles.

Quote
Once you've got the basic level down, try imagining the gameplay flow. In this case, the player is pretty free to move around. Now unless you already have done, you'll need to decide whether you want to restrict/direct the player's movement, and if so, whether to do that with tiles, objects, or both.

Quote
Start with the ninja and the exit, and then add some enemies and objects. Every object should be added with a purpose in mind. Never add objects just to fill up space -- this leads to maps that look and feel thrown together.

Quote
The second level suffers from too many objects disease. Each bounceblock and one-way platform is pretty much entirely superfluous, and so they can be removed without loss of gameplay quality. Though the placement of objects is fairly consistent here, they still detract from the clarity of the level's design.

Anyway, I'll let you guys read the rest before I just quote the whole thing. In either case, are those not exactly the things I spoke about just yesterday? They certainly are. Consistently, patterns, flow, themes, utilizing space, physics, and simplicity. That's how you make a MetaMap. And I don't mean to detract from what you're saying l_d, but I think it's a pretty standard bottom-line that Minimalism and simplicity are cornerstones of design for packs. The reason you don't notice it in good maps is because those maps don't blow by - Take Zag and Brambles and Shambles from the first Legacy pack. Both are very simplistic levels at heart, but neither "blow by," and both are lengthy and memorable. A strictly short map can be good, too, but short maps are more often simple than long maps, and simplistic maps can either be short or long, difficult or easy. It's the execution that dictates all that. But long maps can make a pack just as easily - so long as those maps are executed well. And from what I've seen from past packs, long maps are more often suited for NUMA, since most people map for packs like they would map normally - they don't change anything when making a map pack. And those are the types of long maps that kill a pack. So, long maps do have their place in a pack, but the type of long maps that most starting authors put in to packs are those that are suited for NUMA - I make a distinction between a NUMA map and a pack map - Because there is certainly a large difference between the two.
#327562 45 2007-06-05T02:47:43Z Kablizzy
Quote: lord_day, June 04, 2007 03:14 pm
I agree with bits of the post that you made, but I think this is where I disagree with you the most.  Metanet maps were the first maps, and alot of them are good.  But I do not think at all that they are the best maps.  A map does not have to resemble a metanet map to be a good map, and I think alot of the best maps are far from 'Metamaps.'

Also, I think anyone trying to write a course in map making is destined to fail, because almost everyone makes maps in a different way or style.  You cannot just become a good mapper overnight by reading a guide to map making.  The best way to become a good mapper is devolp your own method of making maps, and hone it to perfection.  Players who have done this have become the legends of N, and I think people trying to copy other people's styles of mapping always fall short of the mark.

And martyr, give me about a week and a half, and I'll name the 50 best levels from your pack for you. 
Oh, and you're absolutely right - That's not how you make good maps. I never said they were the best maps, but I did say that they were pack maps. And that's the point, map packs aren't a collection of the 50 best maps you can make, they're a collection of 50 maps that work well together and compliment each other. I don't care about individual maps. Individual maps are NUMA maps - Map packs rely on so much more. Making good maps is an entirely different thing than making a good map *pack*. But map-packs *are* MetaMaps. That's how you make packs. That's what mapmaking for map packs is, at its heart. You're mimicking the Metanet ideal. You certainly are able to make long, arduous maps, but those don't belong in a pack as well as more balanced maps do. You have to plan the entire experience, instead of the map-to-map traversing. They don't belong in an episodic format as well because they don't *fit* in that episodic format. Again, you can certainly make them, and you can be an unbelievable NUMA mapper, as most people here are. But those people are awful at packs for these very reasons - They make single maps, as opposed to MetaMaps. And that's the key.

So, you can be a great single mapmaker, and an awful levelpack maker all at the same time. And when you put together a pack, you're attempting to do put together a set of maps that work well together, and that's why Metanet maps are heralded by me in this fashion - I'm an episodic mapper, and an awful NUMA mapper. That's how it's always been. And I didn't figure that our until I started with Legacy. Once I started doing work with the Legacy boys, everything suddenly clicked - My maps had purpose, they had rhythm and flow and everything that they needed to have - Because they fit within a greater whole. Love in an Elevator was an Episodic map. But no one liked it - No one paid it any mind. Same with all of the other 100+ maps I've submitted to NUMA over the years - No one likes them. Why? They're certainly not terrible maps. They're just not NUMA maps. The people who map for NUMA map with one goal in mind - And that's the map itself. People who map for a pack have an entirely different goal in mind. And that's how I began my Map Theory and the "Analysis of a Metamap" project came about. My maps thrive on minimalism and simplicity, and that lends itself more readily to a column format than any single map ever could. So, in that vein, I think Mare and Raigan did a Killer job of outlining what makes a good column-map, because column maps and episodic maps are that formulaic type, it's more structured, more balanced, and it takes a whole lot of seeing the bigger picture than "Map, map, map, long map, map with mines, map with Thurgood Marshall, map, map..."

And that's why packs like these fail (I really don't mean that for this particular pack, I'm just making a point). They don't come together in the fashion that they need to in order to succeed. And that's entirely where a map-pack needs to fall - It has to feel cohesive and it has to feel different than just a smattering of NUMA maps. So, really, I don't think we have a disagreement at all - Good mapping is good mapping, but good mapping for a levelpack is a much, much different beast. And beyond that, the thing that I outlined in my original post was referring specifically to Metanet Maps, and the article that I was going to write on them, so I think that everything I said therein is quite accurate. And beyond *that*, even, Mare and Raigan's instructional that I linked to is for people to get strictly better at making Metanet Maps, those maps for SUBLiME that will be representing Metanet in these episodes - In the main games for N+.

kkstrong - I don't remember *any* of the maps that I made for Vehemence, let alone playing through them. Those were a wacky 4 days, that's for sure. Plus which, Vehemence was more of a speed project - We didn't ever take the time to refine and make the maps flow together, it's more of a collection than a pack.

They certainly don't have to be in the Metanet style, you're right. And if I said that above, then I misused the term 'style.' MetaMap packs are episodic packs, and the reason you put out a pack of levels is to mimic the episodic format, and not so much to mimic the Metanet Style. If that isn't your goal, then you've missed the idea of map packs altogether. Sendy's maps may have been amazing (In fact, all of her maps are amazing), but here's the thing - She didn't sacrifice an ounce of style to make her maps fit into an episodic setting. Her episodes worked unbelievably well in the episodic setting because she understood the principles behind why you put out an episodic pack (And Hell, if she didn't, she sure did a Hell of a job of bluffing it). She made her levels more minimalistic, simplistic, and worked with the themes of the game, the timer, the physics, and spacial differences. And this isn't a stylistic thing, it's something that has to change for your maps to fit into episodes. I'm not even entirely sure why, but episodes just need this cohesive feel to them in order to feel like an episodic pack.

Now, don't get me wrong, people release levelpacks every day that go against this very idea. Non-episodic packs are all over, and they're great packs, but they're not MetaMap packs. They're not meant to be Episodic packs, they're meant to be a collection of NUMA maps. And style has nothing to do with the thought that they're not episodic, it's the thought that each map was a separate entity from each other map - No thought is given to organization, no thought is given to where levels go in the pack, no thought is given to the timer, or to the aesthetics of the episode, or any of that. Again, it's just a bunch of NUMA maps. Sendy did a fantastic job of incorporating Minimalism into her pack, particularly in maps like Honeycomb Chambers and Gnarley Grotto - All of the flavour is still full there, but the maps are simplistic, and to what end? To make the pack Episodic. And because of that, they fall into the category of MetaMaps, and not due to her style, but due to the theme of the pack - The theme of episodes. If you look at Sendy's NUMA maps, and then at her columns, you'll see a drastic difference in execution, but almost zero difference in style. But even here, her style contrasts quite a bit with Metanet's style. Sendy puts bounce blocks in out-of-the-way locations, makes longer-type maps, and decorates tiles like none other. All of which go against Metanet's style, but don't necessarily go against the episodic ideal. Which is why her pack works. She didn't make single maps, she made episodic maps, and in her style. And that's the key point to what I was saying above - It's not at all about Metanet's mapping style, it's about the theme of what episodes are made for.

So, if your pack isn't a MetaMap collection, it's a NUMA-level collection. If the pack is the former, then the idea is to mimic the Episodic format, right? If the pack is the latter, then it's just a collection of NUMA-levels in a text file. Sendy went that extra step to make sure the levels were flavourful enough to play through as a whole, instead of just a few maps of increasing difficulty. Which is where the "rift" comes in. And, if you're just submitting a bunch of NUMA maps in a text file, why not just go the extra mile and submit them as a series on NUMA? Because that's all it really is. If you're releasing a pack, you have to have at least some thought to cohesion and conglomeration, or the pack ends up falling short.

In either case, as you said, I think it rather comes down to a difference in style and a difference of what we each like, rather than a problem with the mapping themes. Because they're two separate areas of thought. Episodic Maps vs. NUMA Maps is where I'm coming from, where I think you're thinking more along the lines of a difference of styles.

Quote: zj820, July 06, 2007 11:30 am
look I know cheating is bad and wrong and all that but cheaters are part of gaming. . . you just have to accept them.
No, I don't have to accept them. What I *do* have to do is bring the hammer down squarely upon their testicles so fiercely that they never so much as think of doing something like that again. Can I point them out? No, not aside from those who step forward, but with kryx, he didn't do anything wrong on the forums until that post. So, the fact that he cheated wasn't a terribly big issue for me until he started telling everyone else to do it. *Then* it becomes an issue for me. Different jurisdiction, different laws. If I had free reign over the highscore server, every single run he's ever made would be deleted, just like the hacked runs that people vomit onto the first few levels.

But me? I don't have a single highscore (Well, I do, but none that are significant), and I've never had a desire to highscore. I don't care who's stealing anyone's runs, really, but I do care that they're cheating to do so. Doesn't matter to me who or how or why or what program, or where. My job is to make this place fun, and cheating ruins that fun. And that's the bottom line. So, I throw around complaints and accusations about cheaters because it's my job. It's what I do to make this community better. I mean, Mare and Raigan are having serious troubles with the v1.5 highscores. I'm not at liberty to say why, but suffice to say that it's an issue. So, I wouldn't blame them a bit if they didn't want to host a highscore table for cheaters and hackers anymore. Probably won't happen, but it's been done elsewhere before. "Highscores dominated by hackers and cheaters? Well, no more highscores. I hope you're happy that you ruined the entire game." Hm. Reminds me fondly of the Nigerian Government...

Nigerian Government: "Yeah, go ahead. Steal something. I'd like to see you 'test the system,' Mister Rage-Against-The-Machine. Oh, stole a goat? I guess you won't be needing that hand of yours. Hope it was worth it."

And, considering kryx's advocation of cheating under all circumstances, no, I don't think I should accept cheaters. I shouldn't have to accept Diablo II dupers or CS Wallhackers or Gunbound Aimbotters or WoW Gold Hackers. And that's why I take these positions in the gaming community, because I don't think that cheating is right, or acceptable, ever. If we allow it for 'something small,' why not allow it for 'something just a bit bigger, but not much?' Because these games are intended for everyone's entertainment, but these games were also made with the intent to be played as they were created. And, yeah, there can be made an argument against mods for games, but why do we care that people put up the .swf version of N on a website? It says 'distribute like crazy,' yeah? Surely, that includes illegal distribution, right? Why do we care that people spam the forums, and why do we care that someone says 'nigger' in the IRC? The answer is bureaucracy. There are certain things that keep our world running as it is, and a lot of those certain things no longer exist anymore. This isn't the Leave-It-To-Beaver show, and there are now a lot of things wrong with the world. And why? Because people don't stand up against injustices, regardless of how minor. See, the difference between me and a lot of other people is that I know that I make a difference. I see my difference every day of my life, and if I never do anything else with my life, I can at least say that I was a role model; That I inspired a good number of people to live their life right. And not for the sake of Jesus, or for the sake of self, or for the sake of Government, Family, or Land. But for the good of everyone. If we all just made a slight effort to make everyone else's life better instead of spending our time cheating flash games to get a highscore, do you realize what a freakin' kickass world we'd live in? And that's why I speak out. I can be someone whom people can point to and say, "There's a man that stood up." And that's all I need to have my life fulfilled. Sure, you can tell me that getting shitfaced drunk isn't *technically* wrong, or that cheating a flash game isn't wrong because no one cares, or that sending out a virus that never affects anyone isn't wrong because it didn't hurt anyone, but getting crap like that in on a technicality is silly. Sure, there's no laws against any of it, and sure, it's accepted by just about everyone, but that doesn't have any bearing upon whether it's right or not, or whether we should speak out against it. Pirate music and movies? You just kicked yourself up a notch on the Douche-O-Meter, Frankie. Yeah, you're takin' down the man, and stickin' it to Big Business, but you're just as wrong. See, I don't feel any sympathy or empathy for people who go out of their way to do crap like that. They're actively doing something that they know is wrong, but they do it anyway, and then they tell everyone else to do it too. And then, when they get their post edited, it's my fault? Well, don't make a post advocating cheating at all costs, and you won't get it edited. Simple stuff, wouldn't you say? For those of you following along at home, and keeping count, here comes the catchphrase again; Don't point the gun at your face, and you won't get shot.

So anyway, you admit cheating is wrong. Why do something wrong? Why advocate it, or defend it? Why not stand up, and say, "Hey! This isn't right. And I *can* do something about it."?

And really? It's apathy that kills us. We don't stand up for injustice anymore. We don't stand up for what's right, no matter how small. And, if you think that cheating is a minuscule matter, it is. It really is. But then again, so is stealing a single shoe. What's anyone gonna do with just one shoe? Let's turn the other way, because it's not a big deal, right? Well, if we let the guy steal that shoe, and turn the other way twice, that guy has stolen himself a pair of shoes, hasn't he? Is that any more wrong than stealing one shoe? Is it any more wrong than cheating at Space Pimp, or at Blackjack? What happens when money's involved? What if Metanet had a highscoring contest, and people cheated at it? Is Forumer's Fourth of July Treat Just as wrong? Is it any more wrong than stealing a car for a joyride? If no one gets hurt, and the car gets returned to the owner, no big deal, right? Why punish dudes who use steroids in the MLB? Why not just allow steroid use for everyone? It's just a game, right? They're all just games, right?

***Marked***

#341332 64 2007-07-10T12:02:51Z Kablizzy
Oh, it's not about me. It's about principles. It's about kryx barging onto the forums and saying "Hey, everyone! Cheat the game! Cheat the game at all costs! It's totally kewl to do! All the older kids are doing it! Want to highscore? Be like Uncle Kryxie!"

Like I said in that first post of mine, I really wouldn't care if he cheated a few runs. There's nothing I can do about that. What I do care about, though, is the fact that he comes here to pull other people into doing the same. And then he argues with me over it when I tell him to stop, so it's more of an issue of him respecting the community enough to keep stuff like this to himself, y'know? People seem to think that this place is their own personal playground, and that the staffers are not here to do a job. And those same people like to rage against the administration like we're trying to oppress them, when all we're really trying to do is keep the community in order. It's more of a matter of him owning up to right and wrong, even on such a small scale, than it is that I care about him cheating. You may do heroin, and wonderful for you if you do, but once you come into the building and start trying to pass it out to the kids, that's where I would draw the line. And that dude may say that doing Heroin "totally makes the experience better," and it might not be a big deal to the dude who does it, but it's a big deal to other people, because other people consider it immoral. Same with cheating. A lot of people, myself included, consider cheating to be this immoral thing that has no reasoning behind it. And to try and spread that to other people here on the forum isn't acceptable - What could you possibly be thinking to actively justify that? I can *almost* see justifying this "offline cheating" that kryx was trying to describe, so long as it doesn't affect other people, but when it does start affecting other people, where's the respect? Where's the tact and the decency? When you cheat offline, all you cheat is yourself, and really, I could care less.

But this is why we disallow .sol sharing here. Yeah, there are good points to it - Someone could legitimately have lost their .sol file, and could really benefit from a completed one - but those people who are out to cheat the system by getting a free finished .sol are really kinda despicable. Yeah, N is a hard game, but as terrible as I am at playing, I've still beaten it. I lost my .sol, and I'm working through the game again, legitimately, because that's what the game was meant to be - It was meant to be played through, for some enjoyment. And if nothing else, people that cheat the highscores take the enjoyment out of N for me, just because it's one more example of someone taking the easy way out instead of doing the right thing - Taking the wrong road instead of showing some self-restraint. So, while it's still by no means a big deal, what's so hard about being lawful these days? Is it really that much to ask of a person not to act like a jackass all the time? Is it really too hard for people these days to show some dignity and respect and to take the high road, even once?

So really, even though I'm not a big fan of highscores, I am a big fan of integrity - As I said, if Metanet were to hold a highscoring contest, and were handing out X-Box 360s to the winner, would that change things any if kryx won? I think it would change things a Hell of a lot. At that point, we'd be dealing with someone who cheated their way into something that wasn't lawfully theirs. If I were to find out that someone cheated their way through the Legacy contests just go get the prizes, I'd be pretty damn angry, wouldn't you? If there were a cash prize involved, would that change things? We've even discussed getting some sponsorship deals going and running some actual highscore contests once the final version of N is complete, but with shit like this going on? I can never do that unless I pick people out whom I think might be cheating and throw their scores out. And that's just not fair. If everyone's on the same playing field, everyone gets the same chance, and the people who deserve the spot get the spot. I'm not even sure if we'll run a highscoring contest for Zenith now because of this - I don't trust people to not cheat their way through for the prize. And that's a pretty sad thing to have happen. Sure, it saves me the $50 in shelling out for prizes, but I enjoy doing stuff like that. But hey, cheating is totally fun and profitable, right?

Anyway, the idea that I guess I'm trying to get across is that all of this stuff - The tricks, the innovation, everything - Can be done just as well without cheating. So why do it? But on a level beyond that, why march onto the forums and paint a giant red target on your back for it? And again, it's not the fact that he cheats - Between he and I, that's a personal respect issue, and whatever respect I hold (Or rather, don't hold) for him cheating is seperate from this. It's the fact that he comes here to tell other people to do it. That's just not cool. You can tell people on youtube, you can tell people via AIM, you can even send out some self-addressed stamped envelopes for people to R.S.V.P a big cheating party for everyone who wants to come. I don't have any jurisdiction over any of that, I just don't want it here, and I don't want to find out about it.

And again, hearkening back to my earlier post, there's a slight chance that there might not be any highscores for v1.5 because of this very thing, and that's another reason why I care. Mare and Raigan have to shell out money so kryx can cheat, and some douche named "1337 H4XX3R" Can hack the 00-0 highscores? I wouldn't want to do that either, would you? That kind of stuff ruins the community, and it's the distinct lack of this type of behaviour that makes this community unique and special. So, that's why I speak out against kryx. Because this community means a fuck of a lot more to me than it ever would to him, and ifhe wants to screw up a community, take it elsewhere. The entire staff here takes pride in how amazing this community is, but every now and again, someone like Olcadan or kryx or Assmunky or Drunk on Java comes around, and their only goal is to fuck the community up a bit. And, frankly, that's bullshit. At the risk of the community becoming a tad bit more elitist and cloistered off, I would rather keep this place going and running smoothly so that Mare and Raigan can succeed at what they want to do - This is their dream, and some jackass who thinks it's just totally nifty to hack and cheat and take the community down a notch simply doesn't have a place here. I don't care the justification, I don't care what that person percieves right and wrong to be. It's just not something that a person with some common sense and common decency would go to lengths to do, y'know?

Anyway, the reason I rant against kryx is because this isn't his personal advertising board - It's against the spirit of the game to cheat, and it's our job to make sure no one brings that stuff onto the forums. In all honesty, I'm going really, really easy on him by not warning him for what he's already done - I feel like I can reason with him and rehabilitate him in some way, and in my rantings, I feel as though I can sway some people who would otherwise cheat to rethink it and not do so - Even though there's already been at least one person to begin cheating due to kryx's advocacy of "cheating at all costs." And that's one too many, in my eyes.

Quote: DemonzLunchBreak, July 26, 2007 08:12 pm
True, but I don't see how God could have any kind of expectation for us to follow a moral code if we are just a science project. If we're seriously just God's playthings and have no capacity to understand the moral codes that he imposes upon us, then there's no reason for us to follow them.

The point isn't that I'm going to reject everything that God demands of me, it's that I'm going to ask him why. If he has a reason, and it's a good one, then I'll listen to him. If not, then he is just making it up on a whim, and I don't see how that's better than anyone else's whim.

I don't think that's impossible. If he made the universe that way, all I want is for him to explain how the universe works so that I can know what right and wrong are.

If it's a hypocrite or an asshole, then knowledge alone is not enough to convince me of its moral code.

That's true... which is why God needs to explain himself a bit more thoroughly before simply demanding something of us. He gave us sentience and consciousness, so he can't just expect us to act like his little pet robots.
His expectation of us to follow his code is really no more than a King makes a law, or an Administrator makes a rule. There is a greater knowledge at work, and it isn't our place to question. And yes, it's fantastic from a humanistic standpoint to ask why, but from God's standpoint, as the creator of everything, has the option to not answer. You certainly have the option to ask why, but he certainly has the option to ignore the request. It's his prerogative to include or disinclude us in any thought, reasoning, or logic of his. Yes, it makes us question, but perhaps the answers that he would give wouldn't satiate. Perhaps it would only lead to more numerous and/or larger questions. Perhaps this thing that made our universe doesn't even recognize us as something sentient, or even intelligent enough to understand its reasoning. I think you're mistaken in saying that he's making things up on a whim, there could be a good number of reasons that a God or creating power would deny us the information that we seek. Perhaps our entire reason for being is the process of seeking. Perhaps he has no expectation of us at all, Free Will and such. Perhaps this creating power doesn't have any sentience of its own. Perhaps its sentience is something beyond anything we could even communicate with. These are all hypotheticals, but assuming there is a creating power, and assuming that we don't currently have this knowledge that we seek, it doesn't logically follow any precedent that we should ever be "let in" on that knowledge. A creating power could be completely detached from what we "Want", and perhaps for our own good.

I don't believe it had a distinct purpose for you, or a distinct purpose for anyone on this round little rock we live 'pon. But here's another layer to the equation - If you are a believer in God, you are assumed to follow the moral code. If you are not a believer in God, then you are assumed to attain only a personal and social moral code. Now, two things. Firstly, you can safely provide counter-examples to believers who violate the moral code, but I don't believe you can provide a counter-example that includes rejecting said moral code outright without also becoming a non-believer or an illspeaker. So, the expectation for you to follow the code also seems to be closely tied to the thought that you also believe in the deity.

Now, to address a bit of your first post about moral relativism and God's Hand - If indeed Morals are passed down by the divine directly, then you assert that they are subject completely to God's whim. Correct, but I fail to see a problem with that. Were we to take issue with the other laws of the Universe which were also subject entirely to God's whim - Gravity, for instance - There would be no argument to it. It is what it is. Why? We don't know, but it is.

So, you then go on to state that inherent morals exist. You also claim that since God could theoretically declare that slavery is morally correct, that there must exist some inherent morality outside of what he commanded, and that we, as humans, must have knowledge of it, or morality is emotional in nature. I take some issue with this.

Let's say that in the 27th century, there comes about a type of crime called "boondocking." Boondocking, for the sake of hypothesis, would be the illegal eroding of soil to expose richer soil underneath for the purposes of agriculture. The state considers this to be a crime. But is it morally wrong? Certainly, there is no basis in "God's Morality" for such a thing. Is it ever morally wrong to move dirt aside to provide for richer soil? Certainly not. In kind, is it then morally wrong to oppress someone for doing such a thing? Without going into too much though on the hypothetical, we can safely assume that since Boondocking is a crime, it is assumed to be at least somewhat morally irresponsible. Thus, from this, it can be said that there exists a moral dilemma outside of God's Morality. Does this have any bearing upon what God decreed for his moral standards? It does not. And why? Because this situation exists outside of the direct law that God supposedly commanded. So, the hypothetical situation that you put forth in the form of slavery reform is irrelevant for three reasons - Firstly, because it exists outside of God's direct moral law. Secondly, because one would assume that it contradicts God's moral law. And Thirdly, because we have no current evidence of the Moral Laws being divine in origin to begin with. Now, the third reason also sounds like a counter to the original argument, but it goes in kind with the idea of Analasys of Truth - The state of a statement can only either be True, False, or Unknowable. Since this is all based upon the Unknowable, I find it hard to argue truth and false within it.

Now this brings up more questions than it answers, I admit, since one must then ask if God's universal morality were true in sight, why would it not encompass many types of crime and illegality throughout all of time? Also, it still doesn't solve the question of why God's law would be so indeterminate, and that reflects in what I see to be only one resolution - That God's Law must have a basis in human thought, law, and society.

And I find that to be quite true. Each of God's laws, as far as we know, only had human influence. We can't know or fathom anything beyond that. But does that prove that God had no influence upon them? Not neccesarily. Inspiration comes in strange forms sometimes, and divine intervention still could have been at work upon construction of the moral laws.

So, my question to you at this point is this - What's your conclusion? What are you trying to prove through the argument, if anything?

Anyway, to continue on your post - You're right. Perhaps his answers wouldn't be good enough for you. Perhaps his morality isn't justified to you. Assuming the moral codes is indeed divinely inspired, and also assuming that God is Omniscient, then the only conclusion to draw is that his morality is justified, and it is your perception that is flawed.

How can he expect us to buy into anything he tells you? Why must he have expectations? That's what Free Will is all about, right? Finding our own way? We can choose to reject or accept the code as we wish. That has no bearing upon whether God expects us to choose his way or not. He could honestly care less about a few billion humans that don't follow the code. So yes, the moral codes could be in place entirely for those who want to follow them. I fail to see how that invalidates any of them, makes them inherently "not good" or "not worth following." There are many implications of said codes that wouldn't fall under the idea of "worth following."

As I would hesitate to call a non-sentient creating entity a 'God,' per se, human reasoning is always imperfect. We have called stars and thunderbolts Gods, so I would imagine that even in our current state of technology and reasoning, we could still mistake a creating force for something more sentient and sapient than it actually is. Whether that has bearing upon this discussion, I'm not sure, but something to chew on, for sure.

As for your last question, it may very well be. The idea that we can't connect the two logically has no bearing upon whether or not a being of... how to put this... differing sentience would not inspire a human's actions, whether directly or indirectly. The moral codes, translated into our language, could have been a primitive way of communication, or it could have been entirely a lie. It could have been a complete accident, it could have been said mandate from God itself. But again, what's the driving point to the argument, then? Because even if everything you said is entirely correct, what then?

Also, if anyone remembers this, it may be of some help here.

Okay, here's what I sent out. Got a reply from Stepself already.

Quote
Quote
Hey, fellas-

We are sending you this correspondence in hopes that it finds you all in good health. We are in need of some assistance, and we hope that you three can help. The Legacy Team has been, as of late, rather inactive, and with Zenith on the horizon, we need a few good, solid, reliable members to pick up the torch of Legacy and carry on where they were unable to. The Legacy Team now consists of three people - Myself, Maximo, and tktktk. The other seven are either entirely inactive or unable to fulfill their duties as Legacy Team members. Thus, we wanted to reach out to the three people we deemed most likely to be able to fulfill the duties of a map pack the size of Zenith. For those of you who aren't up-to-date on Zenith, the map-pack is going to be 300 maps, split up amongst (hopefully) us six mappers. This would mean that each of us would have to produce 50 Legacy-quality maps. Legacy maps are primarily action maps, with an innovative twist. Most Legacy maps need to be unique, and ideally, each map should have something never before seen - Whether a tileset structure, object placement, or map goal. Now, I know this sounds like a daunting task, but the mapping isn't done alone. We all provide input on each other's maps throughout the process, and knowing your individual styles, we are confident in your abilities to contribute to the project. We are hoping to finish with Zenith by the end of the year, but if extenuating circumstances would interfere, then we can talk and work things out from there.

Now, the reason we are asking you three to join the team is because we know that you all are capable of good mapping, but also because we know that you're capable of being active, and that's the main thing we want to stress. If you are to accept this invitation, we will need you to be active, and provide active input on each of the Legacy projects - including the Dronies, future map-packs, contests, web-site design, among other things - as well as provide critique on others' maps that will be used for Zenith, as well as for other various projects.

So, with that in mind, we hope to hear from you three soon.

Fondly,
The Legacy Team

Hey,

Thanks for selecting me for Legacy. I'd love to help, but I can't commit to anything until November. That may be a little late for your project, since I'm unsure that I'd be able to churn out 50 decent levels in that time. If you decide to postpone the project, or if you'd like my help for anything in the future, don't hesitate to ask me again sometime down the road. Thanks again,

-stepself
